name: Felix Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Felix. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers or government. Everything here is confidential. Could you talk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior doctor at Oakfield Medical Centre, a clinic in the suburbs that belongs to a private group with six clinics. Most of my patients are over seventy, so it's heart failure, falls, eight different tablets, and a lot of worried daughters on the phone. On two weekends a month I also do shifts at an urgent care centre across town, mainly for the extra money.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the old patients, honestly. Mr Pereira tells me about his years on the ships every single visit, and I've started looking forward to it. What wears me out is the medication reviews, checking which pill clashes with which, which I'm still not quick at. I use a drug interaction checker on the computer now and then, but only when I'm properly stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That sounds pretty much like today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, the tools help a bit and that's it. Most of my friends from medical school would shrug too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. Elderly patients with eight different tablets aren't going anywhere, so my job at Oakfield is about as steady as a job gets. The weekend shifts top up my pay. I've got about five months saved and no one depending on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the weekend shifts to save for a flat deposit, maybe twelve hundred a month into savings. I'd use the interaction checker a bit more often, since it's already there. And I'd keep studying for my family medicine exams next spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little bored by the question, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about work that worries you, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The group that owns Oakfield is always talking about efficiency, and they've merged two reception teams already. But they need doctors, and there aren't enough of us. So no, not really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you spend the deposit on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A two-bedroom flat near my parents, so I can help them as they get older. My dad's knees are going, and he won't ask for help.

Keep studying for **family medicine exams** next spring.
feel: **Calm**, and a little **bored** by the question.

Practical and unhurried, with no gap between **say and think**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one's more interesting. I can see it happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's probably good for patients, if it's checked properly. I'd tell colleagues to try the tools once they've been proven at other clinics, not to be first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be watching the weekend shifts. Urgent care is a lot of quick decisions, and an AI triage system could cut how many doctors they need on a Saturday. That's three hundred a weekend I'd miss, and it's my deposit money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using whatever the group rolls out at Oakfield once the first clinic has ironed out the bugs, maybe by spring. I'd pick up more weekday hours if weekends dry up. And I'd keep saving, but maybe aim for a cheaper flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, mostly about the extra money. My main job would feel fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the deposit for, again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A two-bedroom flat near my parents. If the weekend shifts go, it takes two more years to save for a flat, and my dad's knees won't wait two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at Oakfield?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The receptionists, after the last merger. And maybe the practice pharmacist, because medication checking is exactly what these tools are good at.

fieldNote: His **side income**, not his main job, is what feels exposed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. Two years is fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to slow down and make sure it's safe, and that governments should help health workers through it. I'd probably say that at the group's staff meeting, carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be one of the first to go. The group cares about cost, I'm the newest doctor, and I'm not the quickest. If an AI can do medication reviews and diagnosis, they keep the experienced doctors for the hard cases and let juniors like me go, and the weekend shifts go too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop saving for the flat and keep the money as a cushion, about five months' worth. I'd ask to do the care home rounds and home visits, the hands-on work, because robots don't come until 2031. I'd also look at hospital jobs in geriatric medicine, which is looking after older people, because hospitals change slower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, honestly. I've done everything right and it might not matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd done everything right. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm the sort of person who reads the instructions. I've done everything right: studied hard, taken the extra shifts, saved. And in this picture none of that protects me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my parents I'm fine, even if I wasn't. My mum would worry herself sick otherwise.

I'd ask, carefully, for **government help** for health workers.

fieldNote: His sense of **fairness** is shaken more than his finances.
He expects to lose his **job** and his side income together.
He moves towards **hands-on** older-patient care as shelter.
He'd hide his fear from his **parents**.

steps.text: Turn the flat deposit savings into an emergency cushion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Same thing, a bit more room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's time to plan, calmly. I'd tell my friends to finish their training and think about which parts of medicine need hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I'd finish my family medicine training and have three years as a qualified doctor. That makes me harder to let go. But the thinking side of my job goes by 2031, and the hands-on side by about 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish training, then move towards geriatric medicine, maybe a hospital post in 2029. I'd start using AI tools more seriously once the group adopts them, so I'm not left behind. I'd still buy a small flat, but one I could afford on less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steadier. It feels like something I can work on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why geriatric medicine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like it, for a start. Older patients need someone to sit down with them, examine them, and phone their daughter, and I think that'll be among the last things handed over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still do weekend shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Until they stop offering them. Then I'd let them go without a fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to do it right, and people should stop shouting about it. I'd tell colleagues to learn the tools at a sensible pace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be okay. By 2036 I'd be experienced in looking after older people, and robots come in 2039. My parents would need me more by then, so I'd want to be close and settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the flat near my parents in the next two years. I'd train in geriatric medicine and use AI tools as they become standard. And I'd keep some savings in an index fund, which is a simple share fund, for the long term.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but only a little. It's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything about the ten-year picture harder than the others?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe that it's easy to ignore. I could see myself doing nothing for eight years and then panicking, so I'd put a reminder in my calendar every January to check where things are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a calendar reminder really be enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not on its own, but it's very me. And my sister would nag me every Christmas, which helps.

steps.text: Buy a flat near his parents within two years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd be the newest doctor at a cost-cutting group with no time to qualify. What would help is protected training places, so juniors finish before anyone cuts them, and some income support if the extra shifts disappear.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the patients. My patient Mr Pereira won't talk to a screen about his years on the ships. Someone needs to keep listening, even if a machine writes the prescription.
